entities.summary:
Pasion (d. c. 370 BCE) was a slave in classical Athens who rose to become a wealthy banker and naturalised citizen—one of the best-documented cases of social mobility in the Greek polis. Starting in a money-changing operation, he gained trust managing deposits and loans, earned manumission, and eventually received citizenship for public services, founding a banking house continued by his son Apollodorus.

Speeches in the Demosthenic corpus, especially those involving Apollodorus, preserve vivid detail on Pasion's credit networks, shield factory, and liturgical contributions. His career shows how metic and freedman capital could underwrite Athenian military and civic finance even in a society ideologically jealous of citizen privilege.

Pasion remains a central exhibit in economic histories of Athens: slavery, banking, and citizenship intersecting in the fourth-century commercial city.
